en: And say, ‘Here is the enemy who came!’
To Esenkhan, pillar of heroes,
Say, ‘We have avenged the ancient wrong;
The enemy who stood against us
We have left without descendants.
Not merely three generations, but six,
We have utterly avenged.’
Go and tell this to the great lord.
Ask as a reward for the gold-bearing mines,
The lands where tea is grown,
And the slopes of Khan-Jailak,
And claim them as your due.
You are one Burut against our multitude—
Fight on without turning back!”
So saying, Chongbilgich
Stiffened the resolve of the fainthearted,
And drove them on with sharp exhortations;
Those of his best men who never retreated
Chongbilgich chose and sent forward.
He praised his champions
And drove them into battle.
Once authority gave its command,
Would they turn and merely stare?
Once the great lord’s order had come,
Would they fail to charge where they were told?
Would the champions stand and watch?
The champions now surged forward.
When they had surrounded him,
The champions numbered eighty,
All who remained alive;
When they sprang into battle,
Chongbilgich came behind them,
Driving them forward and clearing their path.
The champions who obeyed the command
Advanced straight upon Seytek
To capture him alive.
Those casting lassos ran forward,
The spearmen plunged into turmoil,
And those who cast iron nets
Circled and drew near,
All advancing together and loosing their bows.
The bowshots cracked,
And as death drew near,
Far from fearing, Seytek rejoiced;
The peerless Seytek stood firm.
From every side they drove their spears
Against him with pounding blows.
The splendid gray wolf, heir of his grandsire,
Neither flinched nor twitched,
Nor faltered or stirred.
He rang like steel, unconcerned,
Counting the assault of all eighty
As less than the hem of his garment;
He struck down everyone he met,
And laid flat those whose death had come,
Waging battle without mercy,
Locked with them in combat.
Chongbilgich, who had given the order,
Now entered the battle in earnest.
Charging with a battle cry,
He did not cease from wreaking havoc.
From the side
The madman came spurring in;
The earth churned and blinded the eye,
As the masterful Bilgich raised his war cry
And bore upon Seytek riding Kulansur,
Just as he was about to reach the beleaguered lion…
Akjoltoi, who had suffered grievously,
Was standing atop a hill.
For the legacy left by his grandsire,
For the son left by his father,
In the poor hero’s pouch
There was medicine for every need,
Every sort of remedy was there.
There was also the meer herb
To feed a thoroughbred steed.
If he fed it the meer herb,
Kulansur, ridden day and night,
Would lose his breathlessness,
His body would ease and recover,
And his argali-like eyes would open wide.
The peerless steed proved a true companion,
Showing the worth of comradeship.
The wounded Akjoltoi
From the medicine for every need
Took two cow-head-sized bowls of black remedy,
And when he crushed and drank them both,
Life stirred visibly within him.
Through his twelve limbs and thousand veins
The medicine coursed everywhere;
His wound closed without pain,
His eyes, sealed like paste, opened,
His vigor returned and strength filled him,
Energy surged and power blazed;
For the gray-wolf hero Joltoi
Good fortune gathered upon his brow.
It was as though he roamed Ala-Too,
With games by day and delight by night;
Life and vigor surged within him,
His belly was full and his blood replenished.
The poor hero could no longer stand watching.
Without setting foot in the iron-soled stirrups,
He leapt astride the thoroughbred Kulunsur,
Mounting him in a single bound.
Embers could not pierce it when tamarisk burned,
Bullets could not pierce it when cannon fired,
Blades could not pierce it in close combat:
The noble Külnaary
Had bitten and worked that wretched armor.
So that in battle against an enemy
No shot would ever stray through,
She had folded it like a serpent’s belly;
The noble Akbermet,
Leading the women with brass thimbles,
Had them stitch it with tiny, even stitches.
Any who worked poorly were rebuked,
Their steel needles were filed anew,
And broken ones cast in the appointed place.
It was stuffed and quilted by champions,
So when a spear was thrust skillfully,
It slid away to one side.
It had nine fastenings,
The blue battle coat worn by champions,
A stout coat no arrow could pierce;
When its wearer entered close combat,
It shepherded his entrusted life,
And when he entered a shooting fight,
It shielded that entrusted life.
Its broad skirt of steel had no opening,
A fitted blue battle coat,
And Joltoi donned it without shaking.
He calmly arranged its buttons,
And tied the fastenings down each side
Without haste or flurry.
Studded with jewels,
It satisfied the heart of all who saw it.
All eyes turned when he girded it on,
And souls rejoiced at the sight;
On a moonless, overcast night,
It shone as brightly as moonlight
When seen upon his waist.
He girded on the blue pouch,
Took up the blue-lacquered spear,
And rode along the edge of the road,
Making the peerless steed Kulunsur
Prance beneath him.
Your hero Joltoi
Rode proudly, braced for battle,
Swaying as though the earth struck toward him,
His silhouette rising like another mountain,
His whole body surging with power.
He shouted from the front,
“Where is my dear Seytek?”
And raised a mighty battle cry.
Seeing strife, battle, and turmoil,
Seeing coats without end,
Joltoi saw the vastness of hell:
Those ninety there, these two here,
Attacking from every side.
With no thought of truce,
And no mercy for precious life,
A fierce battle and great calamity raged;
Spears shattered and heroes fell,
And the turmoil grew immense.
They fought with spears,
Raising piercing cries and hoarse shouts
With all their might.
Seytek rode through, striking as he went,
And any foe who happened to fall,
Akjoltoi cut off his head.
Joltoi rode through, spearing as he went,
And any man he felled, without leaving him whole,
Seytek cut off his head.
They fought, scarcely pausing for breath,
Wreaking calamitous havoc;
When their spears broke and were lost,
They took up their battle-axes.
The falcons who confronted one another
Struck in turn,
Standing face-to-face;
Valuing their fleeting lives not a hair,
They utterly renounced them,
Standing firm for honor,
Fighting without wavering,
Until the tumult became immense.
Mighty Bilgich grew furious:
“We are ninety-four, and these are only two!
Have our strength and endurance departed?
Has all our might abandoned us?
All of you close in and attack!
If grievous death
Is written upon your brow, then face it;
Can a doomed man turn death aside?
Can a brave man with a warrior’s sash
Turn back from death?”
Shouting to embolden them,
The savage Chongbilgich once more
Drove all who remained alive
Into the fray in a surging mass.
He trampled and shattered the battle line,
Scolding all his champions,
Whirling his spear in a rushing arc.
The madman thundered,
Making the wide world seem narrow,
Showing a back as dreadful as hell,
Steeling courage as vast as a mountain,
Working mysteries no man could fathom,
Making his wit, cunning, and strength
Keener than anything in the world.
He dimmed the light and blinded the eye,
Toppling mountains and darkening the sun,
Raising a tumult equal to hell;
Caught in his fury,
The age grew cramped and disordered,
The earth clouded with dust and mist,
And hill, cliff, and lofty mountain
Vanished as though beneath snow.
The weather broke and turned to winter,
So fierce a storm he raised.
Ask no more of Chongbilgich:
A master horseman and swift runner on foot,
Ready and supremely skilled with the spear,
A consummate master of cunning,
His father was the marksman Kojozhash;
Watch his stratagems closely,
And when all means fail, flee.
His onslaught had deep-rooted force,
No living soul survived his bow,
And no creature could withstand
His terrible aspect and venom.
The earth darkened and the waters surged,
So masterful was the battle.
Riding twin gray steeds,
Wearing splendid, mighty coats,
The heroes Seytek and Akjoltoi
Were borne onward by their guardian spirits,
Who raised their hands in aid.
The spirits of their forefathers
Bore them mightily onward.
Without so much as blinking,
The wrath of great Bilgich
The gray-maned hero heeded not, though it would drain him dry;
They fought in turns,
Neither yielding to great Bilgich’s fury
Nor to the venom he unleashed,
Standing firm without submission.
The incomparable Akjoltoy
Had saddled Kulunsur.
Every spell known to man,
He recited without omitting one.
Great Bilgich, the mighty sorcerer,
Sent forth an icy wind,
Splitting the blue-gray sky apart,
Wrapping everything in mist and confusion.
But Akjoltoy was a true champion:
He made the beguiled sun appear,
